extracted.intended_audience: researchers of science communication, press officers, science journalists, and anyone evaluating or producing health- and biomedical-related press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis rubric and analytic protocol for coding exaggeration, caveats, justifications, advice, and human-inference in press releases, associated peer-reviewed articles, and resulting news stories about biomedical and health-related research. Includes sampling, inclusion/exclusion, coding locations, categorical scales, and analysis choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice level (4-category scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each source was coded for maximum level of advice out of four possible categories: no advice, implicit advice, explicit advice but not to the reader or general public, or explicit advice to the reader or general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: implicit advice — 'for adults with a BMI greater than 35 kg/m2…permanent calorie reductions of more than 500 calories per day would be needed…'; explicit but not to reader — 'clinicians must exercise caution in their use of aflibercept'; explicit to reader — 'patients who are at increased risk of cardiovascular events should consider starting statin treatment promptly and continuing it long-term'. A set (journal article, press release and news) was included in the advice analysis if at least one source contained implicit or explicit advice (N=247; 411 news stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal claim strength (7-level scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases, news articles and journal articles were coded for the strength of the main statement of findings according to seven levels: no statement, statement of no relationship, correlational, ambiguous, conditional causal, can cause, and causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding targeted the main statement in title and the first two sentences of news and press releases, or the abstract and discussion in journal articles, because main claims are typically stated first and likely to have largest influence on readers. Analysis focused on studies based on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal designs (intervention/qualitative/simulation designs were excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non-human research (3-category)
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal articles based on a non-human sample, the associated press release and news article were coded for whether findings or conclusions were stated as explicitly non-human, implicitly human, or explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are applied to studies on animals, cells, or simulations. Low N limited some analyses; partial results reported separately. The coding compared press release/news wording to the associated journal article baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (message creep vs journal article baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration was defined as claims or advice in press releases or news that were coded at a level above any of the associated statements in the peer-reviewed paper (i.e., 'exaggeration beyond any that might already exist in the peer-reviewed paper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The peer-reviewed journal article was always taken as baseline. This definition records message creep beyond the journal article text rather than attempting to judge whether the journal article itself contains exaggeration. Example: news makes a causal claim but the journal article did not. Analyses used generalized estimating equations and odds ratios to assess associations between exaggeration in press releases and exaggeration in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of caveats (for causal claims and for explicit advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveats to strong or simplistic claims (e.g., 'We still need more research to clarify whether vitamin D directly prevents bowel cancer…') and justifications for the strength of conclusions were coded for press releases and news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because caveats are rare, datasets from journal press releases were combined with previously collected university press releases for analysis. Caveats for causal/correlational statements were coded for every relevant press release (N=428); caveats for explicit advice were coded where explicit advice appeared (N=188). Presence of caveats was compared to news uptake and to caveats appearing in resulting news; odds ratios reported (e.g., caveats in press releases strongly increased likelihood of caveats in news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of justifications (for causal claims and for advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justifications (statements that justify the strength of a claim) were coded when press releases contained explicit statements of relationship (for causal statements) or explicit advice (for advice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifications for causal statements coded when press release contained any explicit statement of relationship (N=355); justifications for advice coded only when explicit advice present (N=188). Analyses examined association with news uptake and with presence of justifications in news (odds ratios reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding location rule for 'main statement' assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: For press releases and news stories, the main claims were coded from the title and the first two sentences; for journal articles, coding used the abstract and the discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: first two sentences in news/press releases typically state the main claim and are likely to have the largest influence on readers; the focus is on main statements rather than supporting text further down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and selection criteria for sample
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases were identified based on possible relevance to human health, psychology or neuroscience from a predefined set of leading journals for a specified year; press releases were collected from public repositories, journal web pages, or press sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals sampled: Lancet, BMJ, Science, Nature, Nature Neuroscience, Nature Immunology, Nature Medicine, and Nature Genetics for entire year of 2011. News articles were identified from Nexis, BBC.co.uk, uk.reuters.com, and Google searches. Resulting dataset: 534 press releases with associated journal articles and 582 news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion rules for specific analyses (advice/causal/non-human)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses were conducted only for press release–paper–news sets where the relevant content existed: advice analysis included sets where at least one source had implicit or explicit advice; causal claim analysis included press releases and papers based on correlational designs; human-inference analysis included only non-human studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample sizes vary by subanalysis (e.g., advice N=247 sets, causal claims N=164 sets, non-human N=112 press releases). Some analyses could not be performed or were partial due to low N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-coding and inter-rater reliability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A randomly selected subset of press releases and associated news stories were independently double-coded by a different research assistant to assess reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study 147 press releases (27.5% of sample) and 144 news stories (24.7% of news sample) were double-coded, yielding a concordance rate of 98.3% (κ = 0.97). Authors note that where concordance is high and resources are limited, increasing sample size may be statistically preferable to more double coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake measurement (binary and count)
rubrics_metrics.description: News uptake was measured both as whether a press release had any resulting news articles (binary) and as the number of news stories per press release (count).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons of news uptake (press releases with and without associated news) used bootstrapped 95% CIs and standard inferential tests (no clustering). Differences in number of news stories per press release were reported with CIs. Analyses tested whether exaggeration, caveats, or justifications affected news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design inclusion/exclusion for causal claim coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal-claim analyses focused on correlational cross-sectional and longitudinal study designs and excluded qualitative, intervention, or simulation designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction ensures assessment of whether correlational research was misstated as causal; sample for causal claims included 164 press releases and 237 news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis method for clustered data (GEE)
rubrics_metrics.description: To adjust for clustering of several news articles per press release, generalized estimating equations (GEE) were used to determine percentages and 95% confidence intervals for exaggeration rates and to estimate odds ratios for associations between press release exaggeration and news exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GEE with an exchangeable working correlation was employed. For comparisons of news uptake (binary with no clustering), bootstrapping was used for 95% CIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding granularity and instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding was performed using a detailed coding sheet of 191 questions covering statements and other content of press releases, journal articles and news stories; many questions applied only when relevant to the specific press release content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding was manual (research assistants recorded by hand specific information). Each set required 3–4 hours to code; the entire dataset required substantial researcher time (~700 full days). Full coding sheets and instructions are made available in the open data repository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational principle: use journal article as baseline for 'exaggeration'
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer-reviewed journal article is taken as the baseline against which press releases and news are compared for exaggeration; the study does not attempt to judge absolute scientific accuracy of the journal article itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note caveat that if journal articles themselves contain exaggeration, total exaggeration rates would be higher; this operational choice is deliberate to measure message creep beyond the article text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and interpretation cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize limitations of retrospective correlational design, possible unmeasured confounds, and the low base-rate of some phenomena (e.g., caveats), which can affect interpretation and generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution that associations may be circumstantial or mediated and that only experimental manipulation can definitively answer causal influence questions. Also note limited number of sampled journals and that not all journals issue press releases.
